title: Animations and Transitions
subtitle: Bring websites to life with smooth, purposeful motion
description: Learn to create smooth transitions, transform elements, build keyframe animations and make motion more accessible.

blocks.text: PAGE 1 — Animations and Transitions: concepts and applied practice

blocks.title: 1. Introduction to CSS Motion
blocks.text: CSS transitions and animations make websites feel more responsive and engaging. A transition smoothly changes a property from one value to another when a change occurs, such as hovering over a button. An animation can run through several stages defined by keyframes. Both can improve the user experience when used carefully. For example, a button might change color when hovered, while a notification might gently fade into view. Motion should support the content, not distract users or slow down their tasks. In this lesson, you will learn when to use transitions, transforms and keyframe animations.

blocks.title: Example 1: A Smooth Button Transition
blocks.code:
<style>
  .button {
    padding: 12px 22px;
    border: none;
    border-radius: 8px;
    background: #2563eb;
    color: white;
    cursor: pointer;
    transition: background-color 0.3s ease, transform 0.3s ease;
  }

  .button:hover {
    background: #1d4ed8;
    transform: translateY(-3px);
  }
</style>

<button class="button">Explore Courses</button>
blocks.explanation: Hover over the button to see the effect. The transition smoothly changes the background color and position-related transform over 0.3 seconds. Without a transition, those property changes would normally happen immediately.
blocks.output: Hover over the button to see the effect. The transition smoothly changes the background color and position-related transform over 0.3 seconds. Without a transition, those property changes would normally happen immediately.

blocks.question: What does transition: background-color 0.3s ease do in this example?
options: It changes the background color every 0.3 seconds forever.
It smoothly changes the background color over 0.3 seconds when its value changes.
It delays the entire webpage from loading for 0.3 seconds.
It makes the background color change only when the page scrolls.
blocks.explanation: A transition controls how a property change is animated over time. Here, the background-color change takes 0.3 seconds with an ease timing curve.

blocks.title: 2. Understanding Transition Properties
blocks.text: The transition property can control four things: which property changes, how long the change takes, the timing function and the delay before it begins. For example, transition: opacity 0.5s ease-in 0.2s means the opacity transition lasts half a second, uses an ease-in timing curve and waits 0.2 seconds before starting. Common timing functions include ease, linear, ease-in, ease-out and ease-in-out. linear uses a constant rate, while the ease options vary the rate over time. You can transition several properties by separating their definitions with commas. Prefer transitioning specific properties instead of using transition: all everywhere, because broad transitions can animate unexpected changes.

blocks.text: PAGE 2 — Animations and Transitions: concepts and applied practice

blocks.title: 3. CSS Transforms: Move, Rotate and Scale
blocks.text: The transform property changes how an element is visually positioned or shaped without changing the normal document flow. translate() moves an element, rotate() turns it, scale() changes its visual size, and skew() slants it. You can combine multiple transform functions in one declaration. For example, transform: translateY(-4px) scale(1.02) moves an element upward and enlarges it slightly. Transforms are often useful for interactive buttons, cards and icons. Be careful with large movements or scaling, because they can overlap nearby content or feel distracting. A transform changes the element's visual appearance; it does not automatically move other elements out of its way.

blocks.question: What is an important characteristic of transform: scale(1.1)?
options: It increases the element's visual size to 110% without changing normal document flow.
It increases the element's width by exactly 1.1 pixels.
It adds 1.1 seconds to the animation duration.
It moves the element down by 110 pixels.
blocks.explanation: scale(1.1) visually scales the element to 110% of its original size. Transforms do not normally change the element's space in the document flow.

blocks.title: 4. Keyframes: Create Full Animations
blocks.text: Use @keyframes when you want to describe an animation with multiple stages. Give the animation a name, then define what should happen at different points. The from and to keywords represent the beginning and end, while percentages let you define intermediate stages. Apply the animation with the animation property or its individual properties. Important settings include animation-name, animation-duration, animation-timing-function, animation-delay, animation-iteration-count and animation-direction. For example, animation: fadeIn 0.6s ease-out 1 runs a named animation for 0.6 seconds with an ease-out timing curve and one iteration. A keyframe animation can run automatically without a hover or click. Use repeated or infinite animations only when they have a clear purpose.

blocks.question: What is the purpose of @keyframes in CSS?
options: To define the stages of a named animation.
To create a media query for smaller screens.
To set the spacing between flex items.
To make an element respond only to keyboard input.
blocks.explanation: @keyframes defines the stages an animation passes through. The animation property then applies that named animation to an element.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Animations and Transitions: concepts and applied practice

blocks.title: 5. Duration, Delay and Repetition
blocks.text: Animation duration determines how long one iteration takes. Animation delay determines how long the browser waits before starting. Animation iteration-count determines how many times the animation runs; use infinite only when continuous motion is intentional. Animation-direction controls the playback direction, with values such as normal, reverse, alternate and alternate-reverse. The alternate value plays forward on one iteration and backward on the next. The animation-fill-mode property controls how keyframe styles apply before or after the animation. For example, forwards retains the styles from the final keyframe after the animation finishes, while backwards can apply the appropriate starting keyframe styles during the delay. These options give you control over when an animation starts, how often it runs and what remains when it ends.

blocks.question: What does animation-iteration-count: infinite do?
options: Runs the animation once and keeps its final frame.
Repeats the animation continuously.
Waits forever before starting the animation.
Makes the animation duration equal to zero.
blocks.explanation: The infinite value repeats the animation continuously. It does not control the delay or make the duration zero.

blocks.title: 6. Motion, Performance and Accessibility
blocks.text: Professional animations should be smooth, purposeful and comfortable to use. For many simple effects, transform and opacity are good starting points because they can often be animated efficiently by the browser. Animating layout-heavy properties such as width, height, top or left may require more layout work, depending on the effect. Test performance instead of assuming every animation will be smooth. Also consider people who prefer reduced motion. CSS provides the prefers-reduced-motion media feature so you can reduce or remove nonessential motion when a user has enabled that preference on their device. Avoid rapid flashing, excessive movement and animations that make essential content difficult to read. Motion should enhance the experience rather than block access to information.

blocks.question: Why should a developer consider prefers-reduced-motion?
options: It automatically makes all images responsive.
It lets the design respect users who prefer less motion.
It makes every animation repeat infinitely.
It forces all transitions to last exactly one second.
blocks.explanation: prefers-reduced-motion allows styles to adapt to a user's operating-system or browser preference for reduced motion. It does not control image sizing or require infinite animations.

blocks.title: 7. Putting It Together
blocks.text: You now know how to create transitions for changes triggered by interactions, use transforms to move or resize elements visually, and define multi-stage animations with @keyframes. You have also learned to control timing, delay and repetition, and to consider performance and reduced-motion preferences. For practice, create a course card that lifts slightly on hover and a welcome message that fades in when the page loads. Keep the effects subtle and make sure the content remains readable. Test your page with a mouse, keyboard and a touch screen where possible. Remember: a transition describes how a property change happens over time, while a keyframe animation describes a sequence of stages that can run independently of a property change triggered by the user.

blocks.question: Which statement best distinguishes a CSS transition from a CSS keyframe animation?
options: A transition smooths a property change, while a keyframe animation can define multiple stages and run on its own.
A transition can change colors, while a keyframe animation can only move elements.
A transition requires @keyframes, while a keyframe animation cannot use opacity.
There is no difference; both properties must be triggered by hover.
blocks.explanation: Transitions interpolate property changes over time. Keyframe animations define named stages and can run automatically or repeat without requiring a hover event.

blocks.question: Which CSS property would you use to rotate an element visually?
options: transition-duration
animation-delay
transform
animation-iteration-count
blocks.explanation: The transform property supports rotate(), translate(), scale() and other visual transformations. The other options control animation timing or repetition.
